brief_text: We+re deciding whether to move our 40-person support team to a 4-day week next quarter. Current annual support cost is £1.8m and our CSAT is 87%. Do not let CSAT drop below 85% — that is a hard limit for the board. Total implementation spend must not exceed £250,000. Our ops lead thinks productivity will fall 10-15%, but the pilot data from our Manchester office showed a 4% rise. We+d keep hiring flat either way. Success = a 4-day week that holds CSAT at or above 85% and lands within the £250,000 implementation budget. Go ahead.

coaching.summary: The decision is well-structured with clear constraints and a defined success criterion, but the causal chain between productivity change and CSAT needs more scrutiny, and the conflicting productivity signals deserve explicit treatment before moving forward.

bias_signals.detail: The brief says 'Go ahead' after presenting directly contradictory productivity evidence ('ops lead thinks productivity will fall 10-15%' vs 'pilot data showed a 4% rise'), suggesting a conclusion may have been reached before the conflict is resolved.

Success is defined solely as 'a 4-day week that holds CSAT at or above 85% and lands within the £250,000 implementation budget', which frames the status quo option as a non-success by definition rather than as a genuine alternative to be evaluated on equal terms.

The current CSAT of 87% and the £1.8m annual cost are stated as the baseline, and the hard floor of 85% is set just two points below — the proximity of the floor to the anchor may understate how little margin exists if productivity falls as the ops lead expects.

elements_considered_but_excluded: Customer response-time or queue-depth factor — relevant but not named in the brief, so excluded to avoid inventing structure
Regulatory or employment-law constraint — plausible but absent from the brief

strengthen_items.label: Surface the conflicting productivity evidence explicitly
strengthen_items.detail: The brief names two directly contradictory signals — the ops lead's expectation of a fall versus the Manchester pilot's rise — and the decision logic should force a deliberate reconciliation of these before any rollout option is evaluated, since productivity change flows directly into CSAT and the hard floor.

strengthen_items.label: Connect productivity change to implementation spend
strengthen_items.detail: If productivity falls, mitigation measures (tooling, scheduling, overtime cover) would consume implementation budget, yet the current structure treats productivity change and implementation spend as independent paths — closing this gap would reveal whether the two hard constraints can be simultaneously satisfied.

strengthen_items.label: Clarify how productivity change translates into CSAT movement
strengthen_items.detail: The brief states CSAT must not drop below 85% but does not specify the mechanism by which a productivity shortfall would move CSAT, so making that causal pathway explicit — e.g. through response times or resolution rates — would let you test whether the hard floor is genuinely at risk under each option.

strengthen_items.label: Examine what the status quo costs over time
strengthen_items.detail: The status quo option currently flows only into adoption level and implementation spend, but labour market conditions already influence staff retention — making the ongoing cost trajectory of staying on five days explicit would prevent the status quo from appearing artificially low-risk by comparison.

strengthen_items.label: Confirm the direction of the CSAT limit
strengthen_items.detail: You mentioned 85% for CSAT. I couldn't tell from the wording whether that's a floor (keep it at or above 85%) or a ceiling (keep it at or below 85%), so it isn't being enforced yet. Add it as a constraint to make it binding.
